new_statements.translation: Bangwa is a language in which tone plays a very important role in differentiating words and grammatical constructions. Bangwa is thus a tone language, i.e. it uses variations in voice pitch for distinctive purposes. Only vowels and the syllabic nasal can bear a tone. In the tonal register of this variety we noted two level tones: high ... and low ...; to these two level tones are added two melodic or contour tones: rising ... and falling ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Nda'nda' (Bangwa/Batoufam and the other village varieties) is described purely as a tone language: lexical and grammatical H vs L, contour LH/HL mostly in grammatical contexts, a grammatical super-high (upstep) and downstep. No opened description assigns word stress or accent to any position; the only remark touching stress (Gueche Fotso 2021: 12-13) says loanword stress is replaced by Nda'nda' tones.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes: contour tones and the super-high tone do not occur on nouns/verbs in isolation, only in grammatical constructions (Nguendjio 1989: 77-78; Toukam 2021: 22).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical/grammatical tone on words in isolation and in constructions; most native words are monosyllabic (CV, CVC, NCV(C)), polysyllables being mostly compounds and loans (Toukam 2021: 23-24), so a word-stress rule is scarcely at issue in the descriptions. Gueche Fotso 2021 §4.3.1: 'English, pidgin-English and French words are pronounced with Nda'nda' accent. This is only possible thanks to the substitution of stress and accent for tones.'
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is from Nguendjio 1989, which describes Bangwa (báŋgwà, village Bangoua, Ndé Division), an East Nda'nda' (Undimeha) variety; Glottolog files Nguendjio 1989/2014 under ndan1241. Gueche Fotso 2021/2024, Hyman 2017 and Toukam 2021 describe Batoufam/Tswefap, also East Nda'nda'. Ndawouo 1990 = Bangou (shingu), Ngueyep 1988 = Bamena (mɛ̂nɔ̀), other Nda'nda' village varieties. Glottolog mis-codes Chumbow & Nguendjio 1991 'Floating tones in Bangwa' (JWAL 21) to yemb1246 with the note 'What does Bangwa refer to?'; the article itself locates Bangwa in Ndé Division, Southern Bamileke, i.e. Nda'nda', not the Fontem Bangwa (Ngwe/Yemba area).

new_statements.translation: The Bangwa language is a language in which tone plays a very important role in differentiating words and grammatical constructions. Bangwa is therefore a tone language, that is, it uses variations in voice pitch for distinctive purposes. Only vowels and the syllabic nasal can serve as tone-bearing units. In the tonal register of this dialect we have noted the existence of two level tones: high (32) sák 'bird'; low (33) kà 'basket'. To these two level tones are added two melodic or contour tones: rising (34) ɔ̌ 'what?'; falling (35) ʃɛ̂ 'here'.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the very work already excerpted in existing_statements (same passage, same page p.76 / PDF 85); the catalog entry 'Bangwa' has an empty rule and the existing statement reads 'tone language, no stress statement'. Re-reading the whole thesis text layer confirms that reading: nothing on word stress anywhere in the 391 pages. The description is of the Bangoua village variety (gwa de Bangoua), which the author classifies (pp.14-15, after ALCAM code 980) as a variant of the Nda'nda' subgroup, North-East branch alongside Batoufam (twafap) and Bandrefam (danfap) — i.e. the ndan1241 languoid, not the Bangwa/Nwe of Fontem (ngwe1238).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-stress rule is given. The thesis describes Bangwa as a tone language with two level tones (H, L), two contour tones (rising, falling) that are grammatical rather than lexical, and a super-high tone that the author says has no phonological value (p.80: 'ce ton n'a aucune valeur phonologique') and never appears on nouns or verbs in isolation. The words 'accent', 'accentuation', 'intensité', 'proéminence' never occur in a phonological sense; the only 'accent' hits are the idiom 'mettre l'accent sur' (emphasis, in the aspect chapter) and the only 'stress' hit is inside a quotation of Faraclas (1984:14) about Obolo, which Nguendjio cites only to compare sources of a super-high tone, without attributing a stress pattern to Bangwa.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal notes: the HB and BH schemes are unattested on disyllabic verbs (p.78); the super-high tone arises from a low tone under the influence of a floating high in grammatical constructions (pp.79-83).
new_statements.identity_note: Nguendjio 1989 describes the speech of the village of Bangoua (Nde division, West Region, Cameroon), which the author himself, following ALCAM (zone 9, code 980), places in the Nda'nda' subgroup, North-East branch (twafap of Batoufam, danfap of Bandrefam, gwa of Bangoua), calling báŋgwà 'une variante du ndà'ndà'' (p.15). This is ndan1241 (Nda'nda'), not the homonymous Bangwa/Nwe of Fontem, Lebialem (ngwe1238); our earlier reading's ngwe1238 folder already parked the Nguendjio articles as 'not_ngwe_eastern_bangwa_ndanda'.
